title: Academic Discussions — Seminars & Office Hours
story_context: It is Week 5 of the semester. Ahmed's BUSA 301 seminar meets with only twelve students and Professor Reyes, who runs it Socratic-style: no lectures, just discussion. Ahmed has done every reading. He knows the answer to every question. But he cannot figure out how to join the conversation. Jake talks easily, using half-formed thoughts. Zoe interrupts people (politely, apparently). Priya asks questions that make the professor smile. Ahmed speaks twice in ninety minutes — and both times it comes out too long, too formal, and the room goes quiet in a way that suggests everyone was waiting for him to finish. After class, Ahmed goes to Professor Reyes's office hours for the first time.
objectives: Use academic hedging language to contribute to seminar discussions with appropriate tentativeness
Master turn-taking strategies for entering, holding, and exiting academic discussion
Navigate office hours effectively — purpose, etiquette, and how to get the most from them
Distinguish between asserting a claim and exploring an idea in academic discourse
target_phrases: Building on what you said, I think...
It could be argued that the data suggests...
I want to push back a little on that — not because it's wrong, but...
That's a really interesting point — can I add something to it?
I'm still working through this, but my instinct is...
Could we unpack that a bit more?

dialogue.title: Office Hours
dialogue.context: Ahmed knocks on Professor Reyes's office door, fifteen minutes into office hours.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Professor Reyes? I apologize for the interruption. I wanted to discuss my participation in the seminar, if you have a moment.

lines.speaker: Prof. Reyes
lines.text: Ahmed! Come in, sit down. You don't have to apologize for knocking — that's literally what office hours are for. What's up?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: I have completed all of the readings. I understand the material. But in seminar I cannot seem to enter the conversation at the right moment. By the time I have formulated a complete thought, the discussion has moved past where I intended to contribute.

lines.speaker: Prof. Reyes
lines.text: That's a really common challenge, especially for students who are careful thinkers. Can I ask — when you do join in, what do you usually do?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: I state my analysis fully and support it with evidence from the text.

lines.speaker: Prof. Reyes
lines.text: And how does the room respond?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: It becomes very quiet. Then someone says 'yeah' and changes the subject.

lines.speaker: Prof. Reyes
lines.text: Okay. Here's something counterintuitive: in seminar, you don't have to say everything you know. A partial thought that opens a question is often more valuable than a complete argument. Have you heard of 'building on'?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: You mean, beginning with what someone else said?

lines.speaker: Prof. Reyes
lines.text: Exactly. 'Building on what Jake said...' — it signals you were listening, it connects the thread, and it gives you a running start. Also: hedging. Instead of stating conclusions, explore them. 'One interpretation might be' is a seminar invitation, not a declaration.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: I see. So the goal is not to be right. It is to keep the conversation productive.

lines.speaker: Prof. Reyes
lines.text: That's it exactly. Also — your written work is excellent. Your analytical instincts are sharp. Don't stop sharing them; just share them as part of the conversation, not as the answer to it.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: I will try. Building on what you said... I think I have been treating seminar like a presentation rather than a discussion.

lines.speaker: Prof. Reyes
lines.text: There you go. That's a perfect seminar contribution. Come back whenever — door's open.

pattern_drills.pattern: Building on... · Can I add to that? · Actually, I want to pick up on... · I was just thinking...
examples: Building on what Priya said, I think the case study shows a different pattern.
Can I add to that? I think the other reading supports a similar point.
Actually, I want to pick up on the framework question — it seems like a lens issue.
I was just thinking about the same thing — and I wonder if the data supports that.
Following on from that, it might be worth considering the counterargument.
pattern_drills.your_turn: Enter this discussion: Jake has just said 'I think the company's strategy was purely profit-driven.' Respond using a turn-taking opener.
prompts: Agree and add supporting evidence using 'building on.'
Gently question his interpretation using 'I want to pick up on that.'
Add a nuance using 'Can I add to that?'

pattern_drills.pattern: It could be argued that... · One interpretation might be... · I'm still working through this, but... · It seems possible that...
examples: It could be argued that the policy prioritized short-term gains over long-term stability.
One interpretation might be that the author is critiquing the framework itself, not just the data.
I'm still working through this, but my instinct is that the two positions aren't mutually exclusive.
It seems possible that the case would play out differently in a different cultural context.
Could it be that the problem isn't the strategy but the implementation?
pattern_drills.your_turn: State your opinion on a course topic using hedged language. Do not state it as certain fact.
prompts: Suggest that a business decision might have been motivated by factors beyond profit.
Propose an alternative interpretation of a case study without claiming it is correct.
Explore a tension in the readings without resolving it — invite further discussion.

pattern_drills.focus: Office hours etiquette — opening, purpose, and closing
pattern_drills.pattern: Opening · Stating purpose · Specific question · Closing
examples: Hi Professor — do you have a few minutes? I had a question about the feedback on my essay.
I wanted to ask about the case study format — specifically whether you want us to use the textbook framework.
I've been thinking about what you said in class and I was wondering if you could unpack it a bit more.
Thank you so much — this was really helpful. I'll incorporate this into my revision.
I'll let you go — I know you have other students. But thank you for your time.
pattern_drills.your_turn: Roleplay going to office hours with one specific goal (grade question, essay feedback, or discussion help).
prompts: Open the conversation politely and state your specific purpose.
Ask a follow-up question using 'could you unpack' or 'could you say more about.'
Close the conversation gracefully, thanking the professor.

listening_exercises.transcript: Professor: Okay, so the Porter reading. What's actually being argued here? Jake: I mean, I think he's saying competitive advantage is basically about positioning, right? Like, where you put yourself in the market. Priya: Building on that — I think the interesting tension is whether position is stable or constantly shifting. Like, his framework kind of assumes a static competitive landscape. Prof: Interesting. Ahmed, you've been quiet — what do you think? Ahmed: One interpretation might be that Porter's model is descriptive rather than prescriptive — he is mapping how competition works, not necessarily recommending a single optimal strategy. Prof: That's a really sharp observation. Can anyone push back on that?
listening_exercises.question: What technique does Ahmed use to enter the discussion?
options: He states a conclusion directly as fact
He asks a question instead of making a point
He uses hedging language — 'one interpretation might be' — to offer a careful analytical point
He summarizes what Jake said

listening_exercises.transcript: Going to office hours can feel intimidating, but professors genuinely want students to come. Here are three things to know. First, come with a specific question — not just 'I'm confused' but 'I'm confused about how to apply this framework to the case study.' Second, be direct about your purpose at the start: 'I wanted to ask about my essay feedback' — don't warm up for five minutes before getting to the point. Third, office hours are not just for struggling students. Using office hours to deepen your thinking on a paper you're already doing well on is exactly what they're designed for. Professors remember students who show genuine intellectual engagement.
listening_exercises.question: According to the speaker, what is the best way to start an office hours visit?
options: Warm up slowly and let the conversation develop naturally
Only go if you are failing the class
Be direct about your specific purpose at the start
Ask about your grade first before anything else

listening_exercises.transcript: Seminar discussion in American universities has an implicit social contract. Everyone is expected to contribute — silence for a full session is noticed. But contribution doesn't mean having the right answer — it means advancing the conversation. The most valued contributions are often questions, not answers. 'Could we unpack that a bit more?' or 'I want to push back on that idea' are more productive than complete well-sourced arguments, because they invite further dialogue. The goal isn't to win the discussion — it's to make the room think harder. Students who do that get remembered.
listening_exercises.question: What kind of contributions are described as most valued in American seminar discussions?
options: Long, well-sourced arguments that prove a point
Complete silence — listening is the primary role
Questions and challenges that advance dialogue and make the room think harder
Agreeing with the professor's points clearly

speaking_tasks.prompt: You are in seminar. The professor has asked: 'Is stakeholder capitalism fundamentally different from shareholder capitalism, or is it just rebranding?' Contribute one seminar turn of 45–60 seconds using at least two hedging phrases and one turn-taking opener. Do not give the 'right answer' — explore the question.
speaking_tasks.example: Building on what I heard earlier about the tension between profit and purpose — I want to pick up on that, because I'm still working through it myself. It could be argued that stakeholder capitalism is genuinely different in intent — the theoretical commitment to multiple stakeholders is a real shift from Friedman-era doctrine. But one interpretation might be that without binding legal mechanisms, the behavioral outcomes are similar. So maybe the difference is currently more rhetorical than structural? I'm not sure — I think it depends on which companies we're looking at. Could we unpack what 'accountability' actually means in that framework? Because that seems like where the real divergence would show up.
sentence_starters: Building on what was said about...
I'm still working through this, but...

speaking_tasks.prompt: Roleplay opening an office hours visit. You want feedback on why your essay argument wasn't convincing to the professor. Open the conversation, state your purpose, ask one specific follow-up question, and close. Record for 35 seconds.
speaking_tasks.example: Hi Professor Reyes — do you have a few minutes? I wanted to talk about the feedback on my essay. You wrote that the argument wasn't fully developed, and I want to understand exactly what was missing. I had a thesis, I had evidence, but something didn't connect — could you unpack what you mean by 'underdeveloped'? Like, was it the evidence itself, or how I was using it to support the claim? ... [pause for imagined response] ... That makes a lot of sense actually — I'll work on that for the revision. Thank you so much, I really appreciate it. I'll let you go.
sentence_starters: Hi Professor — do you have a few minutes?
Could you unpack what you mean by...?

writing_tasks.prompt: Write a seminar contribution (80–100 words) on this prompt: 'Does globalization benefit developing economies or increase inequality?' Use hedging language, at least one turn-taking phrase, and leave the question open for further discussion — do not conclude with a definitive answer.
writing_tasks.example: Building on the Rodrik reading — I want to pick up on the tension between macroeconomic data and lived experience. It could be argued that aggregate GDP growth figures in developing economies mask significant distributional variation: who captures the gains matters as much as whether gains exist. One interpretation might be that globalization functions as an amplifier — it amplifies whatever institutional frameworks are already present. In countries with strong labor protections and governance, it may reduce inequality. Where those frameworks are weak, it could be argued it intensifies existing disparities. I'm still working through whether that's a feature or a design flaw. Could we unpack what we mean by 'benefit'?

writing_tasks.prompt: Write an email to Professor Reyes after your office hours visit, thanking her and confirming what you will do differently in seminar. Keep it semi-formal, 50–70 words.
writing_tasks.example:
Hi Professor Reyes,

Thank you so much for the office hours conversation today — it was really helpful. I'm going to work on entering discussions earlier with partial thoughts rather than waiting until I have a complete argument. I'll also try using 'building on' to connect to what others have said.

I appreciate your time and feedback.

Best,
Ahmed

grammar_focus.title: Academic Hedging — Expressing Tentativeness and Exploration
grammar_focus.explanation: In academic discussion, hedging (expressing ideas with appropriate uncertainty) is valued — it shows intellectual honesty and invites dialogue. Over-confident claims ('This proves X') can shut down conversation. Hedged claims ('One interpretation might be X') invite response. Common hedging structures include modal verbs (could, might, may), distancing phrases ('it could be argued'), and process markers ('I'm still working through this').
examples: It could be argued that the data supports a different conclusion. (distancing hedge)
One interpretation might be that the author is critiquing the framework itself. (possibility hedge)
I'm still working through this, but my instinct is... (process hedge)
It seems possible that the outcome would differ in a different context. (tentative hedge)
Could it be that the real issue is implementation rather than strategy? (question hedge)

grammar_focus.title: Turn-Taking Phrases for Entering and Holding the Floor
grammar_focus.explanation: Academic discussion requires specific linguistic tools for managing conversation turns. To enter: 'Building on that...', 'Can I add to that?', 'I want to pick up on...' To hold the floor while thinking: 'Let me think through this...', 'What I mean is...' To invite response: 'Does that make sense?', 'What do others think?' These phrases are not just polite — they are structural moves in the discussion.
examples: Building on what Priya said, I think there's a tension here. (enter + credit)
Can I add something to that? I think the Porter reading complicates it. (polite entry)
I want to push back on that — not because it's wrong, but... (respectful challenge)
Could we unpack that a bit more? I'm not sure I've fully understood it. (invite depth)
What I mean is — the strategy exists, but the implementation failed. (clarify and hold floor)

grammar_focus.title: Office Hours Etiquette — Language for Professional Academic Interaction
grammar_focus.explanation: Office hours occupy a semi-formal register between classroom formality and peer casualness. They require polite but direct language, specific purpose-stating, and respectful closings. Overly formal language ('I humbly request your guidance') is unusual. Overly casual language ('So I bombed the essay, can you fix it?') is disrespectful. The target is collegial: professional but warm.
examples: Hi Professor — do you have a few minutes? (appropriate, not 'to whom it may concern')
I wanted to ask about my essay feedback — specifically the part about argument development. (specific)
Could you say a bit more about what you mean by 'underdeveloped'? (professional follow-up)
That's really helpful — I'll incorporate this into my revision. (accepting feedback gracefully)
Thank you so much — I'll let you go. (respectful, time-aware closing)

vocabulary.definition: a small class that involves discussion rather than lecture
vocabulary.example: The seminar only has twelve students, so everyone is expected to contribute.

vocabulary.definition: scheduled times when a professor is available to meet with students
vocabulary.example: I went to office hours to ask about my essay feedback.

vocabulary.definition: a document outlining a course's topics, schedule, assignments, and expectations
vocabulary.example: The answer to your question is on the syllabus — check page two.

vocabulary.definition: the central argument or claim of an academic paper or essay
vocabulary.example: Your thesis needs to be more specific — what exactly are you arguing?

vocabulary.definition: an argument made against a position, often used to strengthen your own argument by addressing it
vocabulary.example: A strong essay acknowledges the counterargument and explains why it does not undermine the thesis.

vocabulary.definition: a subtle distinction or complexity that makes something more accurate or complete
vocabulary.example: The analysis lacked nuance — it treated all cases as identical.

vocabulary.definition: to examine something carefully and in detail (academic usage)
vocabulary.example: Could we unpack that claim before moving on?

vocabulary.definition: presenting a difficulty or challenge; not straightforwardly acceptable (academic usage)
vocabulary.example: That assumption is problematic because it ignores the role of context.

vocabulary.definition: a theoretical framework or perspective used to analyze something
vocabulary.example: Through a Marxist lens, the case study reveals class dynamics.

vocabulary.definition: a structure of concepts used to organize thinking or analysis
vocabulary.example: Porter's Five Forces is a useful framework for analyzing industry competition.

cultural_notes: American seminars are based on the Socratic method: the professor's job is to ask questions and guide discussion, not deliver answers. Students are expected to co-create knowledge, not just receive it. This is culturally different from lecture-dominant education systems.

Silence in American seminar culture is uncomfortable in a way that differs from some other cultural contexts. In East Asian academic cultures, silence can signal respect and careful thought. In American seminar culture, extended silence is read as disengagement.

The phrase 'I want to push back on that' is a culturally specific academic move — politely disagreeing with a professor or peer is expected and valued, not disrespectful. The phrase cushions the disagreement while showing engagement.

Office hours usage rates are much lower than professors would like. Many students, especially first-generation and international students, see office hours as confrontational or as a sign of weakness. In reality, frequent office hours users tend to perform better and build better professional networks.

Academic vocabulary has specific uses that differ from everyday meaning. 'Problematic' in academic discourse means 'presenting a theoretical or ethical difficulty' — not 'a problem' in the colloquial sense. 'Nuanced' means subtle and complex, not vague. Knowing these distinctions marks academic fluency.
